speechImpulse.citation: The appraised impulse of hearing a speech in person, on the core's life-change scale. Political persuasion effects from a single message are small on average (Coppock 2023, Persuasion in Parallel, University of Chicago Press), so a speech weighs less than a life event. Spread 0.1 to 0.5. Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): Kept at 0.3. GAME ASSUMPTION: the appraised mood and stress impulse is not measured by any persuasion study; only the downstream stance shift can be checked (about 5 percentage points on policy opinion right after persuasive information, lasting at least 10 days in most cases; 0.7 to 0.8 points on presidential vote choice; Coppock 2023, Persuasion in Parallel, and Coppock, Hill and Vavreck 2020, Science Advances).

speechRetellWeight.citation: Weight on how far the speech moved the listener's stance when deciding whether to retell it; people talk about what affected them (Berger 2014, Journal of Consumer Psychology 24(4):586-607, on word of mouth). Spread 3 to 10. Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): GAME ASSUMPTION kept; no study gives the share who retell a speech they heard (Pew 2024, n = 8,709: 18% discuss political issues a lot with family and close friends, 58% a little).

speechSociabilityWeight.citation: Weight on the listener's sociability (-2 to 2) in deciding whether to retell. Spread 0.25 to 1. Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): GAME ASSUMPTION kept; no study gives the share who retell a speech they heard (Pew 2024, n = 8,709: 18% discuss political issues a lot with family and close friends, 58% a little).

speechKeepPull.citation: The pull of not retelling, against which retelling is weighed. Checked so that some, not all, listeners retell a speech that moved them. Spread 0.3 to 1. Research, October 12, 2026 (data/research/stand-in-figures-2026-10-12.json): GAME ASSUMPTION kept; no study gives the share who retell a speech they heard (Pew 2024, n = 8,709: 18% discuss political issues a lot with family and close friends, 58% a little).
